title: Girls Take the Field! First-Ever Women's Pro Baseball League Opens in Illinois
summary: History was made on a rainy Saturday in Springfield, Illinois. For the first time ever, women stepped onto a professional baseball field as part of their own league. The Women's Pro Baseball League (WPBL) kicked off its inaugural season, and the excitement was electric. Three hours before the first game, hundreds of fans crowded the parking lot of Robin Roberts Stadium. Some came from down the street; others traveled from South Korea and Australia. A teenage girl with a baseball mitt rushed through the gates yelling, "Am I the very first inside?" She was greeted by a bobblehead of Mo'ne Davis, a star outfielder for the Los Angeles Queens. The league has four teams: the Queens, the New York Heights, the Boston Hunters, and the San Francisco Firebells. Players' families flew in from 11 different countries to watch their daughters and sisters play pro ball for the first time. Kids lined up for autographs, beaming as they showed off signed T-shirts and mitts. The opening weekend was full of special moments. Maybelle Blair, a 99-year-old baseball legend, threw out the first pitch. A mascot named Maybelle, designed in her honor, danced between innings. Even the players helped the grounds crew roll up the tarp after rain. The season will last six weeks, all played in Springfield so fans can easily see every team. For many, it didn't matter which team won. They were just thrilled to witness girls finally getting their own professional baseball league.
why_it_matters: This league shows girls everywhere that there is a future for them in professional baseball, a sport that was mostly for men for such a long time.

background_read: Women have played baseball for over a century, but the most famous earlier league — the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League (AAGPBL) — ran only from 1943 to 1954 during World War II. After it closed, there was no full professional baseball league just for women in the U.S.

Maybelle Blair, a 99-year-old former AAGPBL player, has spent decades hoping to see a new pro league for women. Mo'ne Davis became a household name in 2014 when she pitched a shutout in the Little League World Series, proving girls can compete at the highest levels of baseball.

Having all four teams play in one city (Springfield, Illinois) for six weeks helps fans see every game easily and keeps travel costs low — a smart idea for a brand-new league that needs to build its audience.
Article_Structure: WHO: Hundreds of fans, players from four teams (Los Angeles Queens, New York Heights, Boston Hunters, San Francisco Firebells), and baseball legend Maybelle Blair.

WHAT: The Women's Pro Baseball League (WPBL) started its first-ever season with an exciting opening weekend full of autographs, a first pitch by a 99-year-old icon, and even players helping with the tarp.
WHERE: Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Illinois.
WHY: To give women their own professional baseball league after decades without one, and to let girls see that they can grow up to be pro baseball players.

perspectives.perspective: Excited new players and their families
perspectives.description: They feel proud and emotional to finally have a professional league where daughters and sisters can shine in baseball, not just softball.
See this as a dream come true after waiting many years since the old women's league shut down, and hope it inspires the next generation.
Wonder if the league can keep going financially, since new leagues often struggle to find big TV deals and sponsors, which are needed to pay players and grow.
